nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.prompt: During e-file work under the proximal fold, a tech nicks living tissue. Weeks later the new plate grows with a split starting at the base. Which structure was most likely injured?

options.a: The matrix, the growth tissue under the proximal fold
options.b: The hyponychium seal sitting under the free edge
options.c: The distal nail bed where extra length is filed
options.d: Dead cuticle already shed onto the visible plate

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.explanation: The matrix under the proximal fold produces the plate. A nick there is written into every new keratin sheet as a split, ridge, or deformity as the nail grows out. Hyponychium, distal bed, and shed cuticle do not manufacture the plate, so injury there would not start a split at the base of new growth.

distractorExplanations.b: The hyponychium is the distal seal under the free edge; a nick there would not create a split growing out from the base.
distractorExplanations.c: The nail bed under the attached plate supports it but does not produce new plate from the proximal fold.
distractorExplanations.d: Cuticle is dead tissue on the plate surface; injuring it does not change how new nail is formed.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.prompt: A client wants the pale half-moon at the nail base buffed away so red polish sits flush to the skin. What should you do?

options.a: Buff the half-moon hard; it is only leftover surface stain
options.b: Leave it; the lunula is visible matrix, not a stain
options.c: Hide the half-moon under a thick builder overlay bead
options.d: Nip the living base skin until the half-moon is gone

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.explanation: The lunula is the visible portion of the matrix showing through the proximal plate. It is not polish stain. Aggressive buffing over it thins the weakest part of the plate and can injure growth tissue. Leave the lunula intact and apply color without grinding the half-moon flat.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the lunula with surface discoloration; buffing that zone thins plate over living matrix.
distractorExplanations.c: Heavy builder on the lunula still sits on thin proximal plate and does not make grinding the matrix safe.
distractorExplanations.d: Nipping living eponychium is a wound and does not erase the lunula, which is matrix under the plate.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.prompt: At prep the pink living skin at the nail base looks uneven, and the tech reaches for nippers to 'clean the smile line.' What is the correct action?

options.a: Nip the living fold so the smile line photographs cleaner
options.b: Soak the living fold until it sheds the way cuticle does
options.c: Leave living eponychium; only lift dry cuticle off plate
options.d: Open the living seal with a metal bit until it looks neat

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.explanation: The eponychium is living skin that seals the proximal nail. Cutting or grinding it is a wound and a blood-spill event. Only loose, dead cuticle on the plate may be gently lifted. Uneven living tissue is not a reason to nip; protect the seal and shape product around it.

distractorExplanations.a: Nipping living eponychium for a cleaner photo cuts live tissue and breaks the proximal seal.
distractorExplanations.b: Living eponychium does not shed like dead cuticle; soaking it off still injures the seal.
distractorExplanations.d: A metal bit on living base skin opens the seal, causes bleeding, and invites infection.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.prompt: A toenail is thick, yellow, and crumbling, with packed debris and odor under the plate. The client wants a gel pedicure anyway. What do you do?

options.a: Thin the crumbly plate with a coarse bit and seal gel over it
options.b: Offer a salon antifungal soak and still apply the overlay
options.c: Soak, then hide the yellow crumbling edge with dark polish
options.d: Refuse service and refer; this picture suggests onychomycosis

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.explanation: Thickening, crumbling, subungual debris, and odor are the classic salon picture of onychomycosis, not cosmetic stain. Nail technicians do not diagnose or treat fungus. Enhancements trap moisture and spread debris. Stop the service and send the client to a medical clinician.

distractorExplanations.a: Thinning and sealing a crumbling nail traps debris and can spread infection; it is not a salon repair.
distractorExplanations.b: Salon 'antifungal' soaks are outside scope and do not make an infected nail safe to overlay.
distractorExplanations.c: Dark polish hides a medical picture instead of referring; crumbling plus debris is not surface stain.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.prompt: A week after aggressive cuticle nipping, the proximal fold is red, hot, and swollen, and a drop of pus appears. How should you handle the appointment?

options.a: Refuse service and refer; swollen folds with pus are paronychia
options.b: Drain the pustule with a sanitized nipper, then continue gel
options.c: Soak the fold in acetone and wrap it under a tight overlay
options.d: Push the fold harder so trapped product can work itself out

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.explanation: Red, hot, swollen nail folds with pus are paronychia — an infection of the surrounding skin, often after the seal was cut. This is a medical condition. Do not drain, soak in product, or continue the service. Refuse and refer; covering it hides drainage and can worsen infection.

distractorExplanations.b: Draining a pustule is a medical procedure, not a nail service, and spreads contamination on the table.
distractorExplanations.c: Acetone and a tight overlay trap infection against living tissue instead of sending the client out.
distractorExplanations.d: More pushing on an infected fold further injures the eponychium and does not treat paronychia.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.prompt: Several fingernails show pits, salmon oil-drop spots, and distal lifting, but the surrounding folds are not red or swollen. The client is sure it is fungus. What is the best salon judgment?

options.a: Treat it as onychomycosis with tea-tree oil and a gel overlay
options.b: Suspect nail psoriasis; skip the enhancement and refer out
options.c: Call it paronychia because more than one plate has lifted
options.d: File the pits level and cover them with a hard gel overlay

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.explanation: Pitting, oil-drop/salmon patches, and lifting on several nails with quiet folds points more to nail psoriasis than to typical fungus or paronychia. Technicians do not diagnose skin disease. Enhancements can worsen lifting and hide change. Refuse product and refer for medical evaluation.

distractorExplanations.a: Fungus more often shows thickening, crumbling, and debris, usually starting on fewer nails — not pitting plus oil-drop spots.
distractorExplanations.c: Paronychia is inflamed skin around the nail; quiet folds with plate pitting are not that picture.
distractorExplanations.d: Filing pits and covering them hides a medical nail change and can worsen onycholysis.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.prompt: A thumb was slammed in a car door yesterday. The plate is blue-black and throbbing. The client still wants gel. What is the correct decision?

options.a: Drill a small hole through the plate to drain the trapped bruise
options.b: Cover the thumb with dark gel so the visit still looks finished
options.c: Continue service; blue-black color is only leftover polish stain
options.d: Skip service on a painful hematoma and send the client for care

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.explanation: Sudden blue-black color after trauma is blood under the plate (subungual hematoma), not polish or Pseudomonas. Pain means pressure may still be building and the bed or matrix may be injured. Do not drill, cover, or enhance. Refer; a clinician decides if drainage or imaging is needed.

distractorExplanations.a: Trephining a hematoma is a medical procedure; a salon drill through a painful plate is outside scope.
distractorExplanations.b: Dark gel hides an acute injury and can trap pressure against a damaged bed.
distractorExplanations.c: Polish stain is surface yellow or tint without acute trauma and throbbing; this is blood under the plate.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.prompt: A client wants more leverage, so the tech starts packing acrylic under the free edge against the skin at the tip. What should happen instead?

options.a: Stop; packing into the hyponychium breaks the distal seal
options.b: Pack a thin bead under the tip; that is how extra length is added
options.c: Cut the skin seal away so product can sit under the plate
options.d: Prime the underside of the tip so the skin seal dissolves first

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.explanation: The hyponychium is the living seal under the free edge that keeps pathogens out of the nail bed. Product packed against it lifts the seal, invites onycholysis, and can cause infection. Length is built on top of the plate past the fingertip, never forced under the distal skin.

distractorExplanations.b: Length is sculpted on the plate surface, not by packing a bead into the hyponychium.
distractorExplanations.c: Cutting the distal seal is a wound and removes the barrier that protects the bed.
distractorExplanations.d: Primer does not dissolve living skin and must not be used to open the hyponychium.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.prompt: While thinning an overlay, the natural plate turns translucent pink and the client reports a hot sting. What does that signal?

options.a: Keep going; pink color means leftover product is almost gone
options.b: Stop; heat and pink mean you are near the living nail bed
options.c: Change to a coarser bit so remaining product comes off faster
options.d: Buff the pink until the bed is open and the plate can breathe

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.explanation: Pink translucency plus heat means the overlay is gone and friction is reaching the thin plate over the vascular nail bed. Continue filing and you grind living tissue. Stop, cool the nail, and leave a safe keratin layer. The bed is not a surface to 'open' or finish with a coarser bit.

distractorExplanations.a: Pink is the bed showing through thinned plate, not a cue that product still needs to be removed.
distractorExplanations.c: A coarser bit on already-pink plate removes keratin faster and raises the chance of bleeding.
distractorExplanations.d: The nail bed should stay covered; 'letting it breathe' by grinding through plate is an injury.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.prompt: The distal plate has a white air pocket lifting from the free edge with no redness. The client wants the gap filled so the nail looks attached. What do you do?

options.a: Flood builder into the pocket so the plate glues back down
options.b: Clamp a tight wrap overlay to force the plate onto the bed
options.c: File the lifted plate off the bed and rebuild a full nail
options.d: Do not fill the gap; trim the lift and keep moisture out

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.explanation: Onycholysis is plate separating from the bed, usually from the free edge. Filling the pocket traps water and debris and can feed infection. Do not glue, clamp, or grind the lifted plate onto living bed. Trim the separated keratin short, keep the area dry, and refer if the lift spreads or the bed looks unhealthy.

distractorExplanations.a: Builder in an onycholysis pocket seals moisture under the plate and can worsen the lift.
distractorExplanations.b: Forcing the plate down does not reattach it; it adds trauma to an already separated bed.
distractorExplanations.c: Filing lifted plate off the bed injures living tissue and is not a salon repair for onycholysis.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.prompt: After a high fever, several nails grow with a single horizontal groove across each plate. The client asks you to file the grooves out. What is the right response?

options.a: Leave Beau's lines; they mark a matrix pause and grow out
options.b: Grind each groove flat until the plate looks even again
options.c: Treat the ridges as fungus and refuse only the grooved nails
options.d: Nip living tissue at the base to restart a smooth plate

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.explanation: Beau's lines are transverse grooves from a temporary matrix slowdown after illness, fever, or trauma. They are not fungus and they are not a salon defect to grind away. Filing them thin weakens the plate. Document, service gently if the nail is otherwise healthy, and let the groove grow out.

distractorExplanations.b: Grinding a Beau's line thins an already grooved plate and can expose the bed.
distractorExplanations.c: Horizontal grooves after fever are not the crumbling, debris picture of onychomycosis.
distractorExplanations.d: Nipping living matrix or eponychium does not 'restart' growth; it adds injury.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.prompt: After an injury, living skin is tightly stuck onto the plate and will not lift the way ordinary cuticle does. How should the tech treat that adhesion?

options.a: Tear the adhesion off in one piece so the plate looks clean
options.b: Nip it as loose cuticle because anything on the plate is dead
options.c: Do not force a pterygium; living skin needs medical judgment
options.d: Push daily with a metal tool until the stuck skin lets go

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.explanation: A nail pterygium is living skin abnormally adherent to the plate, not loose dead cuticle. Tearing or nipping it is a laceration. Stop, do not force the tissue, and refer if the adhesion is scarring or spreading. Only true cuticle — dry keratin sitting on the plate — may be gently lifted.

distractorExplanations.a: Tearing pterygium rips living tissue and can permanently scar the eponychium and plate.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses pterygium with cuticle; stuck living skin is not dead tissue to nip.
distractorExplanations.d: Daily metal pushing on adherent living skin worsens scarring instead of releasing it.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.prompt: A pedicure client has a red, painful ingrown toenail with swollen sidewall tissue and wants gel polish on that toe. What is the correct limit of service?

options.a: Dig the corner out with a nipper to give the edge more room
options.b: Pack cotton under the edge and cover it with gel for a week
options.c: File the swollen skin down so the nail can grow straight
options.d: Refuse work on that toe and refer for medical care

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.explanation: An inflamed ingrown toenail is a medical problem involving living tissue, not a pedicure correction. Cutting the corner, packing, or filing swollen skin can deepen infection. Skip that toe, do not apply product over the fold, and send the client to a clinician or podiatrist.

distractorExplanations.a: Digging out an inflamed corner is a surgical-style act and risks a deeper infection.
distractorExplanations.b: Cotton plus gel over an inflamed ingrown traps bacteria against the sidewall.
distractorExplanations.c: Filing swollen living skin is not a nail-tech duty and does not treat an ingrown.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.prompt: After weeks of dark polish, the plate is yellow on the surface but still smooth, even in thickness, and free of debris. The client fears fungus. What is the best reading?

options.a: Refer as onychomycosis because any yellow nail must be fungal
options.b: Treat as cosmetic polish stain; fungus looks thick or crumbly
options.c: Recommend a household bleach soak until the yellow lifts off
options.d: Buff the plate very thin so the surface stain disappears

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.explanation: Surface yellow after dark lacquer, with a smooth even plate and no debris, is usually cosmetic staining. Onychomycosis typically adds thickening, crumbling, or packed subungual debris. Do not diagnose fungus from color alone, do not bleach, and do not grind the plate thin; use base coat and let stain grow out.

distractorExplanations.a: Yellow tint alone is not onychomycosis; fungus is a texture and debris picture, not just color.
distractorExplanations.c: Household bleach on skin and nails is unsafe and outside a nail technician's scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Buffing stain off by thinning the plate causes peeling; stain sits on keratin and grows out.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.prompt: After a rushed gel soak-off, the nails peel in sheets, feel paper-thin, and sting with acetone. What most likely happened?

options.a: A coarser e-file next time would have spared the keratin layers
options.b: The matrix died, so these nails will not grow back at all
options.c: Over-filing or ripping product damaged the keratin plate
options.d: Skipping base coat from now on will let the plate thicken

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-na.explanation: Peeling, paper-thin plates right after removal are almost always mechanical damage to existing keratin — over-filing, prying, or forced soak-off — not a dead matrix. Matrix death would change new growth from the base over months. Rest the nails, stop aggressive removal, and keep a gentle base; do not chase thickness with a coarser bit.

distractorExplanations.a: A coarser bit removes more plate, which is how many soak-offs become paper-thin in the first place.
distractorExplanations.b: The matrix sits under the proximal fold; surface peeling after removal is plate damage, not matrix death.
distractorExplanations.d: Base coat protects a thinned plate; skipping it does not rebuild keratin lost to over-filing.
